title: Victoria's new data centre rules – implications for developers and operators
description:
The Victorian Government has released its Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan (Action Plan) which introduces new planning, renewable energy and community benefit requirements for data centres looking to operate in Victoria.
However, the transition to renewable energy is already well underway, with renewable energy developers and data centre operators increasingly collaborating through power purchase agreements.
New referral authorities for data centre applications WorkSafe Victoria, VicGrid, Fire Rescue Victoria and relevant water corporations will become referral authorities for data centre applications.
What does this mean for data centre developers and operators?
If you have any questions about the new rules or would like support with a data centre project, please get in touch with us.
text:
The Victorian Government has released its Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan (Action Plan) which introduces new planning, renewable energy and community benefit requirements for data centres looking to operate in Victoria. These rules include separating data centre facilities from residential areas, new investment in renewable energy and storage that matches their energy use and contributing to local communities.

With more than 50 data centres operating in Victoria, data centres accounting for around 3% of electricity supplied through the National Electricity Market (NEM), and data centre electricity demand in Victoria almost doubling in the 12 months to June 2026, it is unsurprising that the Action Plan seeks to ensure data centre investments are well planned, manage resources responsibly and benefit their host communities.

Location and land-use requirements for data centres

Released on 22 September 2026, the Action Plan sets out land-use and location requirements to keep data centres away from homes and other sensitive uses by prohibiting data centres on residential zoned land and introducing a 150-metre buffer between a home and a data centre. This setback is a substantial change, given that some existing facilities in Melbourne’s west are only 15 metres away from homes.

The Action Plan will not apply retrospectively, so it will not affect projects already underway or being assessed. It will only apply to future projects.

Data centres will also be kept away from productive agricultural land by prohibiting them in rural zones. An exception applies where critical infrastructure capable of servicing the data centre, such as major transmission infrastructure, substations, renewable energy facilities, battery energy storage systems (BESS) or recycled water infrastructure, is nearby.

Noise requirements

Existing industrial and commercial noise limits, including a night-time limit, will apply to new data centres. Where multiple facilities affect the same location, their combined noise impacts will be assessed.

Renewable energy requirements

The Action Plan requires that electricity demand by data centres need to be met by new investment in renewable energy and storage that matches the data centre’s new energy demand.

Data centres in Australia generally run on power from the grid, with backup diesel generators. However, the transition to renewable energy is already well underway, with renewable energy developers and data centre operators increasingly collaborating through power purchase agreements.

Water supply requirements

The Action Plan seeks to protect drinking water supplies by requiring data centres to use recycled water or other non-drinking water sources to cool their facilities, or to transition to these sources when they become available.

Local jobs, training and community benefits

To maximise opportunities to support Victorian jobs, skills and training, the Action Plan requires data centres to provide apprenticeships and traineeships for construction and operational workers, support local suppliers and supply chains, and work with local training providers and employment services to hire local workers.

The Action Plan provides for the development of a Local Investment Guarantee to ensure a data centre development gives back to the community through local employment, skills development, training partnerships, engagement with First Nations communities, local procurement, or improvements to local parks or community facilities.

New referral authorities for data centre applications

WorkSafe Victoria, VicGrid, Fire Rescue Victoria and relevant water corporations will become referral authorities for data centre applications. They will join the Environment Protection Authority, which already holds statutory referral status for these developments.

What are the next steps?

It is anticipated that the Action Plan will be reviewed as conditions evolve. The next steps will include:

development of detailed guidance on location, siting, design and built form, with stakeholder input, in 2027

Commonwealth legislation setting standards for data centres’ use of energy, water and land, expected in early 2027 and to be developed with the states and territories

a Local Investment Guarantee, to be developed with local government and industry

planning scheme amendments to extend mandatory referral status to various regulatory bodies.

What does this mean for data centre developers and operators?

The Action Plan forms part of the growing regulatory framework for data centre developments in response to their rapid expansion in Australia. Melbourne is Australia’s second-largest data centre market and navigating this framework will be an unavoidable part of carrying out these developments in Victoria.

For developers and operators, this makes early planning and property due diligence essential to identifying potential land-use barriers. Planning for the energy needed to meet anticipated demand will also help address any gap between when the digital infrastructure and renewable energy supply will be ready. Early planning is therefore not only part of the application and approvals process but also critical to the success of a data centre project.

If you have any questions about the new rules or would like support with a data centre project, please get in touch with us.

text:
Public electric vehicle charging access is expanding in the NextZero Participant towns of Belmont, Hull, and Ipswich, Mass., the Massachusetts Municipal Wholesale Electric Company reported in the Summer 2026 issue of its Joint Action Newsletter.

The Massachusetts Clean Energy Center (MassCEC) recently announced that $9.5 million has been awarded via grants to help advance climatetech companies across the Commonwealth.

Included in this funding is $311,236 through MassCEC’s InnovateMass Gridtech Spotlight program for an initiative by MMWEC, Belmont Light, Hull Municipal Light Plant, Ipswich Electric Light Department, and Voltpost, a New York-based company that retrofits lampposts and utility poles into a modular and upgradable electric vehicle charging platform.

By retrofitting existing infrastructure, Voltpost provides electric vehicle drivers convenient and affordable charging access while reducing the cost, timing, and footprint of chargers. The grant will allow Voltpost to install its first pole charging stations in Massachusetts.

MMWEC's NextZero program is a residential and commercial/industrial efficiency and electrification program for customers of municipal utilities, designed to provide the most efficient, innovative, and equitable path to energy decarbonization.

“This collaboration with Voltpost, MassCEC, and our municipal light plant partners in Hull, Ipswich, and Belmont is a major step forward for local clean energy access,” says MMWEC Sustainable Energy Program and Policy Senior Manager Zoe Eckert. “By leveraging existing utility poles for Level 2 EV charging, we’re delivering a scalable, cost-effective solution that makes driving electric practical and accessible for our public power communities.”

MMWEC is a not-for-profit, public corporation and political subdivision of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts created by an Act of the General Court in 1975 and authorized to issue tax-exempt debt to finance a wide range of energy facilities.

description:
STOCKHOLM, Sept 28 (Reuters) – A surge in diesel prices linked to this year’s Iran conflict has helped make electric trucks cheaper to own and ​operate than diesel models in six major ‌European Union markets, which account for almost half of the bloc’s new truck sales, according to an analysis by Brussels-based environmental advocacy group Transport & Environment.
• The report, published on Monday, found that electric ‌trucks ​purchased in 2026 generate savings ⁠over five years of ⁠up to €100,000 ($113,910) in the Netherlands, €85,000 in Germany and €69,000 in Denmark compared with diesel vehicles • In those markets, operators can recoup the initial price premium in ​around two years • T&E said rising diesel prices following this year’s Iran-linked oil price spike strengthened the ⁠business case for electrification • Europe’s ⁠electric truck transition has been slowed by ​high purchase prices and patchy charging infrastructure • The report ​examined total cost of ownership in nine EU ‌countries • It found that electric trucks were already cheaper to operate than diesel models in the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, France and Belgium, markets accounting for 46% ⁠of EU heavy-truck registrations.
• Reuters reported earlier this year that European truckmakers such as Daimler Truck, Volvo Group and Traton’s Scania ⁠were bracing ‌for a wave of lower-cost Chinese ⁠competitors, with some Chinese electric trucks expected ​to ‌be priced about 30% below comparable European ​models • T&E ⁠estimated a Chinese-built electric truck costs about €210,000, versus €265,000 for a European equivalent.
• In Germany, operators could save an additional €34,000 over five years by choosing a Chinese-made electric truck.
($1 = 0.8779 euro) (Reporting by Marie Mannes in Stockholm; Editing ​by Matthew Lewis)

text:
SINGAPORE, 15 September 2026 – The global power sector is becoming increasingly central to economic growth as artificial intelligence (AI), digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and the electrification of transport, buildings and industry increase demand for stable, reliable and available power.

At the same time, geopolitical and policy uncertainty, ageing assets, supply-chain bottlenecks and uneven grid infrastructure are shaping the direction and pace of change, according to the latest Power Market Review published today by Willis, a WTW business (NASDAQ: WTW).

Asia’s power insurance market remained highly competitive through the first half of 2026, supported by strong insurer profitability, abundant reinsurance capacity and sustained competition among international and regional insurers. Well-performing power companies continued to secure premium reductions, broader participation and enhanced policy terms, particularly for gas-fired generation, renewable energy projects and operational assets with sound engineering standards and favourable loss experience.

This buyer-friendly market is developing as Asia’s digital infrastructure build-out creates a new wave of power demand. The region’s data centre development pipeline reached a record 26.5 gigawatts in the first half of 2026, with Southeast Asia accounting for about half of capacity under construction[1]. As hyperscalers and AI platforms expand, reliable power supply is becoming a critical factor in markets where digital infrastructure is built, increasing investment in generation, grids, storage and behind-the-meter solutions.

Lyo Foo, Head of Power, Natural Resources Asia, at Willis said: “AI and data centre growth are making reliable power a strategic asset across Asia. As large, concentrated loads expand, risk can no longer be assessed in silos: generation, grids, cooling, water, cyber, supply chains and business interruption are increasingly connected. Power companies that use today’s market leverage to strengthen engineering evidence, stress-test recovery assumptions and align insurance with their growth plans will be best positioned to support the region’s digital infrastructure ambitions.”

Key Asia highlights from the report include:

Capacity and competition remain strong. International and regional insurers are actively deploying capacity, while increased participation from Middle Eastern markets is adding competitive pressure to Asian insurance placements.

Quality risks are benefiting most. Power assets with robust engineering data, disciplined maintenance, credible valuations and favourable loss records are achieving premium reductions, broader insurer participation and improved terms.

Capacity for coal plant is still available for well-managed risks, although insurer scrutiny is expected to intensify over time. This is due to ESG commitments and sustainability objectives of many international insurers and reinsurers. The best insurance outcomes will depend on how clearly insurance buyers evidence risk quality, asset stewardship, transitional plans, maintenance regimes, business interruption exposures and portfolio-level resilience.

Preparation remains critical for 2027. Early market engagement, transparent risk information, together with up-to-date engineering information and clear loss experience will help buyers convert abundant capacity into resilient, sustainable coverage.

Lyo added: “The outlook for the second half of 2026 remains positive. Asia’s power insurance market remains exceptionally competitive. International and regional insurers continue to deploy significant capacity, enabling many clients to secure premium reductions, broader insurer participation and enhanced policy terms. While engineering quality, operational performance and claims history remain important underwriting considerations, insurers’ desire to maintain premium income and expand market share has become the dominant factor shaping renewal outcomes.”

The Power Market Review 2026 examines insurance market conditions, emerging risks and resilience priorities across the global power sector, including a dedicated outlook for Asia.

text:
[DigitalToday Seung-ah Yoo, intern reporter] Hyundai Motor Group reaffirmed its position that it will continue pushing ahead with the development of all-solid-state batteries.

From startups to major automakers, companies are continuing to invest in all-solid-state batteries, touted as a “dream technology” to deliver ultra-fast charging and longer driving range for electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, the performance of conventional lithium-ion batteries is improving quickly. Geely’s latest battery technology takes less than 9 minutes to charge from 10 percent to 97 percent. Even so, is there still a need to keep developing all-solid-state batteries?

On Sept. 27 (local time), EV-focused outlet InsideEVs reported that Hyundai Motor Group R&D chief Manfred Harrer (만프레드 하러) gave a firm “yes” to that question.

Harrer told reporters last week, “We cannot give up now. That is clear,” adding, “We must be part of this competition.”

Current EV batteries use a liquid electrolyte to move lithium ions between the cell’s anode and cathode. All-solid-state batteries, by contrast, mainly replace that liquid electrolyte with a solid material such as ceramics or polymers. This could raise both safety and performance. But no company has yet succeeded in producing solid-state cells at a scale suitable for automobiles.

Harrer cited smaller batteries, improved fast-charging performance and longer driving range as potential advantages of all-solid-state batteries. He forecast that a symbolic vehicle produced in small volumes with an all-solid-state battery would appear within the next 5 years. QuantumScape is also aiming to apply all-solid-state batteries to high-performance vehicles by the late 2020s.

Raw material costs are expected to remain very high for years as the technology scales up. Harrer said this would make it difficult for all-solid-state batteries to enter the mass market. “In the end, you can solve everything, but it costs money. It comes at an enormous cost,” he said.

Hyundai is developing all-solid-state batteries in-house while also working with partners such as Solid Power. Harrer described all-solid-state batteries as “the industry’s big bet right now.” Toyota has been developing all-solid-state batteries for at least 20 years and is targeting mass production within the next few years. Volkswagen is making large-scale investments in QuantumScape, while BMW is working with Solid Power. General Motors, Ford, Honda and Nissan are also moving into all-solid-state battery development.

Some companies have already unveiled demonstration prototypes. Examples include a Ducati equipped with QuantumScape cells and a Mercedes vehicle using Factorial’s technology. But there are still no cases of all-solid-state batteries being fitted in mass-produced vehicles that consumers can actually buy.

Harrer’s goal is for Hyundai to enter the market with its own supply chain and manufacturing capabilities once the technology matures. “We want to be the owner of this key technology,” he said. “That is why we are also investing in our own battery manufacturing.”

Harrer explained that it is important to deeply understand battery manufacturing methods and the associated costs. Batteries are the most expensive component in EVs and are also used in other electrified vehicles. Hyundai plans to apply its in-house nickel·manganese·cobalt (NCM) cells to the extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) version of the Tafe, which is scheduled to launch early next year. In a recent announcement, Hyundai said it plans to launch the Tafe EREV in the first half of 2027.

All-solid-state batteries are expected to take considerable time before reaching the mass market. “I do not think we can solve the raw material cost issue within 5 years from now,” Harrer said.

title: US study finds small reactors can't win on the grid, but can at factories and hydrogen plants
description:
Heavy industry may be where small nuclear reactors make money first, according to new research, even as the technology remains far from transforming the broader U.S. power grid.
The study says the reactors are unlikely to win out in the open electricity market against inexpensive renewables and existing large-scale power generation.

For a broader look at where nuclear technology could gain traction, these stories dig into some of the most plausible paths.
text:
Heavy industry may be where small nuclear reactors make money first, according to new research, even as the technology remains far from transforming the broader U.S. power grid.

The study points to factory complexes that need round-the-clock heat, power, and clean hydrogen in one location as a better match for the technology than direct competition with low-cost renewables or big existing generators.

If that holds, industrial operators rather than utilities could become the earliest serious test case for small modular reactors, or SMRs.

Here's what to know

Sites like ammonia plants, oil refineries, steel mills, and other manufacturers that depend on steady process heat appear to offer the best U.S. market for SMRs, according to a new analysis published in Nature Communications, cited by Interesting Engineering. The study says the reactors are unlikely to win out in the open electricity market against inexpensive renewables and existing large-scale power generation.

To reach that conclusion, researchers from the University of Michigan and Idaho National Laboratory modeled energy demand across dozens of ammonia synthesis plants, nine steel mills, 47 oil refineries, and nearly 1,000 manufacturing sites that rely on process heat.

Industries that already consume significant hydrogen appear to be the most promising early fit. In ammonia production and petroleum refining, SMRs could provide the heat and electricity needed to make clean hydrogen on-site, reducing the costs and risks of transporting such a volatile fuel over long distances.

More background

Under the SMR concept, reactors would be built in a more modular way at centralized sites, then moved by rail or barge and installed in clusters as local energy needs require. That differs from traditional nuclear plants, which are largely constructed on-site through massive, highly customized projects.

The study found that U.S. industrial facilities produced 1,499 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2020. Researchers estimated that replacing some fossil-fuel-based industrial heat and hydrogen with nuclear-derived alternatives could lower emissions by as much as 14% over two production cycles.

Still, the economics remain fragile. The analysis found that these projects become viable much faster when paired with a federal clean-hydrogen tax credit worth up to $1.36 per pound of clean hydrogen.

What's being done?

Researchers found that suitable factory locations could host about 91 gigawatts-electric of SMR capacity in an early phase. As manufacturing methods improve and more units are built, that figure could rise to 171.9 gigawatts-electric.

That kind of rollout could give developers a more controlled environment to test whether SMRs can reliably provide both electricity and high-temperature heat before trying to compete more directly with other power sources. No SMR has entered commercial operation in the United States yet, making real-world demonstration especially important.

Cleaner fertilizer production, refining, and manufacturing could eventually help reduce industrial pollution while supporting domestic energy supply.

The technology may have its strongest chance in applications that reward continuous output and industrial heat, not in markets where wind, solar, and existing power plants already dominate on price.

As Brendan Kochunas, associate professor of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences at the University of Michigan and study co-author, said, "There's a lot of momentum around increased deployment of nuclear energy and small modular reactors, but this study provides the first comprehensive analysis of where it actually makes business sense to build and operate them."

Where can I learn more?

For a broader look at where nuclear technology could gain traction, these stories dig into some of the most plausible paths. They cover the cost challenges facing SMRs, coal-to-nuclear conversions, and other reactor concepts.

• In the U.S., experts will examine serious challenges for SMRs as cost pressures persist.

• Across the U.S., former coal sites could offer nuclear conversion opportunities instead of retirement.

• Advanced reactor developers say molten salt systems could improve safety and flexibility underground.

At NYSERDA, we work year-round to catalyze New York’s statewide energy transition, but for one week in September each year – at Climate Week NYC – the world turns its eyes to New York City to identify the highest priority solutions to fight climate change and build a cleaner, more reliable, and affordable energy system.
For our part, Governor Hochul and NYSERDA brought a few announcements of our own to a jam-packed week of events.
Climate Week NYC is about turning commitments into implementation.
By enabling further growth of our in-state renewables sector, and advancing utility-scale energy storage, we are ensuring an affordable and reliable clean energy transition for all New Yorkers.
As Governor Hochul said at the Ceres climate event last week: “Ambition matters but execution is everything.” Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA
text:
If you were feeling the heat this summer, you were not alone. August 2026 was tied with July 2023 as the hottest month ever recorded on Earth. As we continue to feel the worsening impacts of extreme weather, one thing that is a source of constant motivation is all the colleagues and partners working to advance a clean energy future.

At NYSERDA, we work year-round to catalyze New York’s statewide energy transition, but for one week in September each year – at Climate Week NYC – the world turns its eyes to New York City to identify the highest priority solutions to fight climate change and build a cleaner, more reliable, and affordable energy system. Throughout the week, my NYSERDA colleagues and I had the opportunity to speak before thousands of interested parties and meet with the stakeholders, businesses, and organizations who are collectively advancing this transition.

Something that strikes me the most about the week is the sheer volume of events and the diversity of collaborators involved. From a sustainable rooftop farm in Queens to packed conference halls with attendees from all parts of the clean energy ecosystem and world, Climate Week offered an opportunity for everyone to share, discuss, and learn from each other. We left invigorated and optimistic with new ideas and updates on the incredible progress being made across so many different sectors.

For our part, Governor Hochul and NYSERDA brought a few announcements of our own to a jam-packed week of events. First and foremost, Governor Hochul announced her Clean, Highly Affordable, Reliable, Grid Expansion, or CHARGE agenda – an aggressive framework of clean energy and affordability measures designed to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers while achieving a reliable, zero-emission grid.

Notably, she also announced the Energy Infrastructure Development Plan – which will update New York’s State Energy Plan process with an actionable blueprint designed to align resources with energy demand and economic growth. As chair of the New York State Energy Planning Board, I look forward to reconvening this year to begin the comprehensive and integrated planning needed to address New York’s near and long-term needs through this expanded work.

The Governor also matched last year’s record-breaking climate action investment by adding a second $1 billion installment to the landmark Sustainable Future Program. Governor Hochul also announced that $1 billion in state energy rebate checks designed to help over 8 million New Yorkers who are struggling with higher utility costs and prices at the pumps began going out last week and will continue through December. This is in addition to the State’s aggressive enrollment drive to ensure all who are eligible for the Energy Assistance Program have applied and receive direct utility bill savings. Eligibility was expanded in 2026 and 2.5 million households are eligible.

And as for NYSERDA, we announced that contracts have been executed for 1.7 gigawatts of new large-scale energy resources, including eight bulk energy storage projects and 13 land-based renewable energy projects. Combined, these projects are expected to create more than 1,100 family-supporting jobs and will commit over $3.7 billion in private investment. Through these new projects, we are reinforcing the State’s commitment to the development of locally-produced clean energy, energy storage, grid resiliency and economic development, which are well equipped to leverage federal clean energy tax credits and reduce costs for New Yorkers.

We also travelled to communities like Amsterdam, NY, where we marked the official ribbon cutting of ECOFlats, a Buildings of Excellence Award winning project and announced nearly $135 million to advance design and construction of energy efficient housing. As part of this investment, $100 million is now available to support residential new construction at every stage of development through the State’s New Efficient Homes New York program. New construction projects such as these are an opportunity to integrate the latest high-performance technologies and building solutions into homes and demonstrate how to use energy more efficiently, improve comfort and protect against extreme weather.

Climate Week NYC is about turning commitments into implementation. By enabling further growth of our in-state renewables sector, and advancing utility-scale energy storage, we are ensuring an affordable and reliable clean energy transition for all New Yorkers. I commend Governor Hochul for being a champion in accelerating these projects over the past five years, which helped make us a leader in the creation of clean energy jobs and is spurring economic development opportunities for businesses and local communities across our state.

As Governor Hochul said at the Ceres climate event last week: “Ambition matters but execution is everything.”

Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA

title: Trump Approves Rollback of Fuel Economy Rules, Says Automakers Will Expand US Output
description:
The announcement, made in a post on Truth Social, confirms a proposal first floated in December that would sharply lower corporate average fuel economy, or CAFE, requirements for model years through 2031.
CAFE standards set a minimum average fuel economy for each automaker's full lineup of vehicles sold in the United States.
Tesla (TSLA), the market's dominant electric vehicle maker, slipped about 2%, and electric truck startup Rivian (RIVN) gained more than 1%.
Trump's announcement also highlighted the political stakes of the fuel economy fight.
Any litigation could delay implementation, though the Trump administration has moved aggressively to defend its environmental rollbacks in court.
text:
President Donald Trump said Saturday he has signed off on new fuel economy standards that dismantle the centerpiece of the Biden administration's push to electrify America's vehicle fleet, a move he framed as a lifeline for Detroit automakers and a cost break for car buyers.

The announcement, made in a post on Truth Social, confirms a proposal first floated in December that would sharply lower corporate average fuel economy, or CAFE, requirements for model years through 2031. The Transportation Department is expected to formally publish the final rule on Monday, according to Benzinga.

"I have just approved new Fuel Economy Standards that TERMINATE Sleepy Joe Biden and Pete Boot-EDGE-EDGE's ridiculous EV Mandate," Trump wrote, using his derogatory nicknames for the former president and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

Trump said the new rules will strip what he called wasteful costs out of vehicle production, predicting that sticker prices will fall and that American families will save thousands of dollars on a new car. He also claimed that the Biden-era standards had forced automakers to absorb billions in losses while pushing consumers toward vehicles they did not want.

The president said the rollback has already triggered commitments from major manufacturers to expand domestic production. "Every manufacturer, from General Motors to Ford to Stellantis, has called me wanting to build here, and now they can!" he wrote. He said automotive investments under his administration now exceed $100 billion, with new and expanded plants expected to support jobs in Michigan, Ohio, Indiana and South Carolina.

Trump thanked Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for their roles in implementing the policy. Lutnick has previously credited the administration's tariff regime with pulling manufacturing back to the United States, citing expansion plans at Ford and Toyota Motor (TM).

The new standards represent a dramatic reversal of the trajectory set under President Joe Biden, whose administration had required passenger-car fuel economy to improve 2% annually for model years 2027 through 2031, with light trucks facing similar increases starting in 2029. Those rules targeted an average light-duty vehicle efficiency of roughly 50.4 miles per gallon by 2031.

Under the Trump administration's December proposal, the CAFE target for the 2031 model year would drop to about 34.5 miles per gallon, a reduction of nearly one-third from the Biden-era goal. The final rule approved Saturday has not yet been published in detail, but is expected to track closely with that earlier blueprint.

CAFE standards set a minimum average fuel economy for each automaker's full lineup of vehicles sold in the United States. Higher thresholds effectively force manufacturers to increase the share of electric and hybrid models in their fleets. The Biden administration argued the tougher rules would save Americans more than $23 billion in fuel costs and nearly 70 billion gallons of gasoline through 2050, while preventing more than 710 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

Trump has repeatedly rejected that logic, arguing that aggressive efficiency mandates saddle automakers with expensive technology requirements that inflate vehicle prices and erode profitability. His administration has also moved to unwind federal support for electric vehicle charging infrastructure, a sharp contrast with the previous White House's goal of building 500,000 publicly available chargers by 2030.

Buttigieg, who oversaw the Biden-era standards, fired back at the president's announcement. He said U.S. manufacturing and auto employment have declined under Trump and warned that weakening fuel economy rules would undermine American competitiveness in clean technology, effectively "handing the clean tech future to China" while leaving consumers to pay more at the pump.

The policy shift lands as investors are recalibrating expectations for the auto sector. Shares of General Motors (GM) and Stellantis (STLA) each closed about 3% higher on Friday, while Ford (F) added roughly 1%. Tesla (TSLA), the market's dominant electric vehicle maker, slipped about 2%, and electric truck startup Rivian (RIVN) gained more than 1%.

The divergent stock moves reflect the uneven impact of the regulatory rollback. Legacy automakers with large internal combustion engine portfolios stand to benefit from lower compliance costs, while pure-play EV manufacturers lose a regulatory tailwind that had pressured competitors to accelerate electrification.

Trump's announcement also highlighted the political stakes of the fuel economy fight. The president has made auto manufacturing a signature issue, repeatedly pointing to tariffs and deregulation as tools for reviving industrial employment in the Midwest. He said last month that his trade policies had helped Ford's Detroit plant run around the clock and called it one of the most profitable car plants in the world.

The new standards mark one of the most consequential regulatory reversals of Trump's second term, effectively removing the federal government's most powerful lever for pushing automakers toward electrification. Without stringent CAFE requirements, manufacturers face far less pressure to sell electric vehicles at scale, which could slow the expansion of charging networks and alter the economics of battery production in North America.

Some critics have warned that the move runs counter to global efforts to curb transportation emissions, a concern Buttigieg echoed in his response. The transportation sector is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, and light-duty vehicles account for the bulk of that output.

The final rule is expected to face legal challenges from environmental groups and Democratic-led states, a pattern that has followed many of the administration's deregulatory actions. Any litigation could delay implementation, though the Trump administration has moved aggressively to defend its environmental rollbacks in court.

This isn't simply China replacing Japan as the market is fragmenting, with Chinese, Japanese and Korean makers competing on price, hybrids, software and financing.

text:
ISLAMABAD:

China's automotive industry has set a record this year as vehicle exports have already surpassed last year's total by August. As Chinese automakers expand into emerging markets to offset Western trade barriers and domestic overcapacity, Pakistan has become one of the clearest beneficiaries.

This global push is disrupting a decades-old Japanese auto oligopoly in Pakistan, aided by Islamabad's New Energy Vehicle Policy (NEVP 2025-2030). As Chinese manufacturers expand into high-tech crossovers and electric vehicles, Pakistan stands at a pivotal crossroads: how to leverage Beijing's manufacturing scale to slash its crippling fossil fuel import bill, while avoiding the substitution of one form of import dependence, ie foreign oil, with another: imported batteries, electronics and high-value automotive components.

The central question is, therefore, larger than whether Chinese EVs will displace Japanese cars. It is whether Pakistan can use Chinese technology and capital to move beyond low-value vehicle assembly towards genuine manufacturing, technology transfer, supplier development and eventually exports.

Global supply push

China's total annualised vehicle exports have soared to 12 million units, anchored by 10 million passenger cars. Its new energy vehicle exports, battery electrics and plug-in hybrids combined, have reached an annualised 5.6 million units, eclipsing Japan's historical peak export figures.

This has upended legacy automakers. In just 24 months, Germany's multibillion-dollar trade surplus with China flipped into a deficit. As Western markets impose defensive tariffs, Chinese manufacturers are redirecting capacity towards the Global South. For Pakistan, this creates an unusual opportunity. Chinese firms possess battery, motor, power electronics and software technologies that would take Pakistan decades to develop alone. The challenge is ensuring access that creates domestic productive capacity, not just a bigger market for imported Chinese parts.

Disrupting the 'Big Three'

For over 30 years, Pakistan's car market was dominated by Toyota, Honda and Suzuki, shielded by high tariffs with little pressure to modernise. Macroeconomic headwinds, forex constraints and fuel prices crippled traditional assembly lines, opening the door for new entrants.

Chinese brands, Sazgar Haval, Changan, Chery, BAIC, Jetour, have now captured a share in the SUV and crossover segments, with Haval challenging the Toyota Fortuner. On the electric side, BYD (via Hubco subsidiary Mega Motor Company), Changan's Deepal and budget models like Dewan Honri have pushed EVs from a luxury niche into the mainstream.

This isn't simply China replacing Japan as the market is fragmenting, with Chinese, Japanese and Korean makers competing on price, hybrids, software and financing. Japanese firms retain strong dealer networks and supplier relationships, while Chinese entrants bring faster product cycles and EV capability. The NEVP backs this shift with structure: a target of 30% new energy vehicle sales by 2030, rising to 50% by 2040; 3,000 public fast-charging stations by 2030; a 1-3% carbon levy on combustion vehicles funding EV subsidies; concessional duties on CKD/SKD kits; and a capped charging tariff of roughly Rs40/kWh to absorb surplus power generation.

This matters because Pakistan's electrification push is also an energy-security play. Petroleum imports drain foreign exchange, while the power sector has excess capacity and weak demand. But the net forex benefit depends entirely on how much of the EV value chain Pakistan localises, since a fully imported EV kit assembled locally still increases component imports even as it cuts oil use. Success should be measured in forex savings, domestic value addition, supplier development and exports, not just EV sales volume.

Localisation vs import dependence

The risk is that Pakistan reproduces its old assembly-dependent model with a new technology stack: Chinese tech, imported components and Pakistani final assembly, which is analogous to changing the propulsion system without changing the country's position in the global value chain.

Three factors will determine success. First, manufacturers must be pushed from CKD kit assembly towards local battery manufacturing, parts casting and software integration. This doesn't mean building everything domestically as battery cells and advanced semiconductors need scale that Pakistan can't match. Instead, the policy should target realistic wins: battery-pack assembly, wiring harnesses, castings, plastics, interiors, charging equipment and thermal management.

Secondly, the 3,000-charging-station target needs sustained private investment, grid upgrades and standardised protocols; none of which happen automatically. Low EV penetration makes chargers commercially unattractive, while poor charging infrastructure suppresses adoption – a chicken-and-egg problem. Existing petrol stations could become charging nodes, while battery swapping and fleet charging may matter more for motorcycles, rickshaws and taxis.

Thirdly, Japanese assemblers are introducing their own hybrids to defend their market share, which means more competition that should improve pricing and after-sales service industry-wide.

The bigger opportunity may lie beyond passenger cars. Pakistan's motorcycle, three-wheeler, taxi and commercial-vehicle markets are used intensively and consume heavy fuel, meaning electrification there could deliver faster payback and greater fuel-import savings per rupee of support than premium passenger EVs.

From assembly hub to manufacturing base

The new Automotive Industry Development Policy 2026-31 raises the stakes further, emphasising localisation, investment and exports. The opportunity is to use Chinese manufacturers' search for new markets to strike a deeper bargain: market access in exchange for supplier development, technology transfer, training and export-oriented production.

Pakistan's domestic market alone won't provide the scale for a globally competitive EV industry. The more ambitious goal is integrating Pakistani suppliers into Chinese global value chains and eventually positioning the country as a regional production base. In the end, an exported Pakistan-made component may ultimately matter more than another locally assembled car.

In a nutshell, China has already solved the technological problem of mass EV production. However, Pakistan's challenge is different: capturing a meaningful share of the economic value that EV technology creates. The real story isn't China replacing Japan but whether Pakistan can turn China's automotive rise into a shift from assembling cars for itself to manufacturing products the world wants to buy.

Making Space For Solar Power “Developing solar on constrained parcels is a growing focus for the industry.

text:
Demand for solar power is running hot, and yet space for solar development is increasingly limited by community opposition and government intervention at the federal, state, and local level. Space is at a premium even where the regulatory environment favors solar, particularly in cities and other urbanized areas. That’s where the creativity factor steps in, as illustrated by the US firm Cultivate Power.

Making Space For Solar Power

“Developing solar on constrained parcels is a growing focus for the industry. It’s becoming more important as competitive land use drives solar onto smaller and smaller parcels,” Cultivate explained in an email to CleanTechnica last week.

The company’s latest project is a case in point. The new Bowes Solar array sits on a 22-acre site in Elgin, Illinois. Situated between two residential subdivisions, the site is further encumbered by high-voltage power lines and train tracks. A wetlands area in one corner offers yet another obstacle to conventional solar development.

The Cultivate team tackled the challenge from several angles. To accommodate the irregular footprint of the site, they divided the installation into two arrays for a combined total of 11 megawatts (DC). By dividing the site in two parts, Cultivate also gained the flexibility needed to accommodate setback requirements and avoid impinging on the wetland.

To maximize the solar power potential of the site, Cultivate deployed a high-density racking system developed by the firm Planted Solar.

In addition, the Planted Solar racking system sits low to the ground, helping Cultivate to avoid conflicts related to community aesthetics. With the installation of an opaque fence and additional screening, the panels are not visible from outside of the site.

Solar Power And Community Engagement

Small-scale solar power projects rarely make headlines, let alone national news. However, the Bowe arrray did attract local coverage that fleshes out the picture in terms of the steps solar developers can take to rally local support for their projects, particularly in the area of small-scale community solar.

Community solar refers specifically to solar power plants that directly benefit local communities in the form of reduced electricity costs and increased tax revenues. Chronicle Media, for example, notes that the new Bowes array will benefit ratepayers with lower electricity rates. Distributed through the utility Commonwealth Edison, the lower rate covers the whole area, including 580 low- and moderate-income households.

“Aimed at saving customers 20 percent on energy charges, the project will also benefit several larger customers, including three small businesses, two towns and a church,” notes Chronicle reporter Bill Dwyer.

“Cultivate Power officials say that collectively subscribers will save $13.9 million on their ComEd bills during the next 40 years,” Dwyer adds.

Lower electricity rates are an important community engagement tool, but not the only one. Property tax revenues from the site are also expected to total $2.1 million over the next 40 years, benefiting the local school district and other agencies while making productive use of a property that resisted other forms of development, largely due to the wetlands factor.

The Chronicle further notes that Cultivate is making substantial contributions to Elgin Community College and Food for Greater Elgin (a member agency of the Northern Illinois Food Bank), along with contributions to Friends of the Fox River, We Care Solar, and the Evolve Foundation among others local organizations.

High Density Solar Arrays Are Coming For Your Fossil Fuels

Community engagement aside, the solar technology developed by Planted Solar also played a key role in the Bowes project.

Planted launched on a mission to squeeze the maximum amount of kilowatts out of a small space. The company points out that community solar projects generally require 5-7 acres for each MWp (megawatt-peak), with MWp referring to the theoretical maximum output of the array under ideal conditions. That would mean, for example, that an 11-megawatt array like the Bowes Solar project could not fit into a 22-acre space.

Alternatively, a smaller array could be developed at the site, but then the law of diminishing returns might kick in, killing the project altogether.

Planted addresses the challenge with a software-enabled racking system that requires only about 2 acres per MWp, with the flexibility to fill in irregular spaces that are typically left undeveloped in a conventional solar array. At 2 acres per MWp, a 5-megawatt community solar project would only require about 15 acres of land all together, instead of the 40-50 acres called for under a conventional scenario.

Another conventional rule of thumb is that sites with a slope of more than 10% require grading. Such sites are often automatically eliminated from consideration for community solar projects due to the additional expense of grading. Substantial earthwork can also delay the permitting process or result in project cancellation.

The Planted system addresses that challenge with a terrain-following strategy that accommodates existing grades of up to 27%. “Sites where a landowner wants pasture or vegetation preserved, or where a county has made low-disturbance a condition of approval, are often viable candidates,” Planted notes.

“The site still needs to meet slope and acreage thresholds, but grading restriction alone doesn’t disqualify it,” the company adds.

The Power Of Community Solar

Interested? Community solar planners can use Planted’s online contact form to submit information about their site and received an assessment.

Meanwhile, if you caught that thing about landowners and pastures, that brings up a rural angle of interest. As illustrated by the Bowes project, community solar projects are often associated with cities. Elgin, for example, is one of the biggest cities in Illinois aside from Chicago. However, Cultivate Power’s equity investor, Generate Capital, points out that community solar projects can be valuable assets in rural communities, too.

“In a rural farming community like Mercer County, solar savings are out of reach for renters and low- and moderate-income families who are unable to install their own panels,” Generate explains.

“Landowners, meanwhile, face pressure to keep every acre productive. Community solar answers both, extending savings to local subscribers, while giving a working farm stable new income alongside its crops,” the firm adds.

Generate draws attention to Cultivate’s Goldenrod Solar project, commissioned in Mercer County last year. Though weighing in at just 5 megawatts, the project delivers enough solar power to accommodate 850 local subscribers, with anticipated savings of 10-20% on their electricity bills. As is typical of community solar projects, low- and moderate- income households represent 55% of the subscribers.

The community engagement element of the Goldenrod project also included contributions to local organizations including Black Hawk College Foundation, Sherrard High School, and Mercer County High School Future Farmers of America chapters, among others.

text:
With a broad smile, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva praised the environmental achievements of his third term during a speech on June 10 at the Planalto Presidential Palace in Brasilia. "Brazil has become the country with the most credibility in the world when it comes to environmental stewardship," the 80-year-old president said proudly.

From the moment he took office in January 2023, President Lula established the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples, launched numerous operations against illegal gold mining, replenished a fund dedicated to protecting the Amazon, and revived environmental agencies paralyzed under his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro (2019-2022). Thanks to these efforts, annual deforestation in the Amazon fell from 11,594 square kilometers to 5,731 square kilometers between 2022 and 2025 – a 50% decrease, according to satellite data collected by the National Institute for Space Research.

"The Lula government's legacy is positive for the environmental agenda," said Maiara Folly, the executive director of the CIPO platform, a Brazil-based think tank focused on climate governance. She also welcomed "the central role that environmental issues have played in Brazil's foreign policy." In addition to strengthening cooperation among Amazonian countries, the left-wing president hosted COP30 in Belem, in the heart of the Brazilian Amazon, in November 2025. Brazil used the summit to champion two international initiatives: the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a financing mechanism to protect tropical forests that remains underfunded, and a roadmap aiming to phase out fossil fuels.
